question: With the switch from the Windows 10 to Windows 11 operating systems, technology market analyst Canalys estimates that one third of PCs currently in use (and purchased before 2018), i.e. some 240 million PCs, will become obsolete in the next two years as their hardware features will be incompatible with the new operating system.

This means that despite their processors being sufficiently powerful to perform most functions and support most current programs, these computers are likely destined for the electronic scrapheap, forcing thousands of consumers and public bodies to fork out for new equipment.

Microsoft ceased sales of Windows 10 in January 2023 and PCs with this operating system will receive no security updates or technical support beyond October 2025. The company is offering only one way to escape the upgrade: to enrol in its paid extended security update programme (ESU), available until 2028. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission not think that this move constitutes an abuse of a dominant position that will prove disruptive to consumers and public authorities and disastrous for the environment?
Is it not also at odds with the EU’s ecodesign and reparability goals? Could this not be avoided by simply extending the Windows 10 licences?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.6.2024) EU Competition law does not oblige undertakings, even dominant ones, to ensure that their software can be used on all hardware platforms. Ecodesign regulations implementing Directive 2009/125/EC1 cover ‘physical’ products (and the same applies under the new Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR)) and not software products.

Consequently, the Ecodesign legislation on physical products is not fit for purpose for ‘extending Windows 10 licences’. Moreover, although almost all computers are placed on the market with a ‘bundled’, preinstalled operating system, for the vast majority of computers the supplier of the operating system is a different market player.

The ongoing review of the Ecodesign Regulation on computers, however, may tackle the issue similarly to what is done for smartphones and tablets, by committing the computer supplier to ensure that software updates are available for a certain number of years from the end of the placement of the computer on the EU market2.

Consumer protection law3 requires the sellers of goods with digital elements to ensure that the consumer is informed of and supplied with updates necessary to keep the goods with digital elements in conformity for the period of time that the consumer may reasonably expect given the type and purpose of those goods.

Moreover, the new Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive 2024/825 will ensure better consumer information at the point of sale about the minimum period of software updates for goods with digital elements, for digital content and for digital services4.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32009L0125 2 Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/1670, Annex II, A.1.(6), point 1.2(6) - Operating System updates. 3 Directive (EU) 2019/771 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on certain aspects

concerning contracts for the sale of goods, amending Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 and Directive 2009/22/EC, and repealing Directive 1999/44/EC, OJ L 136, 22.5.2019, p. 28-50. It applies to sales contracts concluded as from 1 January 2022.

4 Directive (EU) 2024/825 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 February 2024 amending Directives 2005/29/EC and 2011/83/EU as regards empowering consumers for the green transition through better protection against unfair practices and through better information. Available at https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/825/oj
